entries.meaning: Surprise someone so completely that they are briefly lost for words.
examples: I was taken aback by how blunt her answer was.
His question took me aback, and I just stared at him.
She looked taken aback when I offered to pay for everything.
Don't be taken aback if he turns the offer down.
The size of the repair bill took us aback.
Everyone was taken aback by how quickly he agreed.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress — took me aBACK
entries.separable: yes — and the object almost always sits inside the phrase: her answer took me aback. With a pronoun it must split: ✗ took aback me. A full noun after the particle (took aback the whole room) is possible but rare.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — and usually in the passive, be taken aback
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but a momentary event of surprising someone, so the progressive is odd: ✗ her answer is taking me aback. It has no linking or stative use.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the usual form — I was taken aback by how blunt her answer was; she looked taken aback. The active her answer took me aback is the marked one.

entries.meaning: Resemble an older relative in looks, character, or habits. It runs one way only: a child takes after a parent, never the other way around.
examples: She takes after her mother — same laugh, same temper.
He takes after his grandfather more than anyone else in the family.
Both boys take after their dad.
I don't take after either of my parents.
If she takes after him, she'll be tall.
People say the youngest one took after his uncle.
entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: быть похожим на, пойти в (кого-то из родни)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: takes after her mother, takes after her. ✗ takes her mother after, ✗ takes her after.
entries.verb type: stative — a resemblance, like resemble itself, not anything the subject does. It rejects the progressive: ✗ she is taking after her mother.
entries.passive: no — a stative resemblance verb, and the prepositional object cannot be promoted: ✗ her mother is taken after by her, ✗ his grandfather was taken after.

entries.meaning: Separate something into its pieces — and, figuratively, do the same to an opponent or an argument.
examples: He took the carburetor apart on the kitchen table.
She can take apart a laptop in about four minutes.
Don't take it apart unless you know how it goes back together.
Our defense took them apart in the second half.
The visiting team took us apart, 42 to 3.
The reviewer took the argument apart point by point.
My advisor took apart the whole third chapter.

senses.head: Dismantle
body: Undo something into the parts it was built from. The opposite is put back together, not take together. (разбирать на части)
examples: He took the carburetor apart on the kitchen table.
She can take apart a laptop in about four minutes.
Don't take it apart unless you know how it goes back together.

senses.head: Defeat completely
body: Of a team or a fighter: beat the other side so thoroughly that they never get going. (разгромить, разнести)
examples: Our defense took them apart in the second half.
The visiting team took us apart, 42 to 3.

senses.head: Pull an argument to pieces
body: Analyze something hostile line by line until nothing is left standing. (раскритиковать, разобрать по косточкам)
examples: The reviewer took the argument apart point by point.
My advisor took apart the whole third chapter.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: разбирать (на части); разгромить; разнести в пух и прах
entries.separable: yes — take apart the engine or take the engine apart, and with a pronoun the object must split the phrase: take it apart, never ✗ take apart it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: dismantling (he's taking the carburetor apart), defeating an opponent, and pulling an argument to pieces.
entries.passive: yes in every sense — the carburetor was taken apart on the kitchen table; we were taken apart, 42 to 3; the whole third chapter was taken apart.

entries.meaning: Lead someone away from a group for a private word, usually a serious one.
examples: The coach took me aside after practice.
She took him aside and told him to stop.
Let me take you aside for a second.
He took aside the two students who had been whispering.
My boss took me aside to warn me before the meeting.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes, and in practice it is nearly always split: took me aside. A full noun can follow the particle (took aside the two students who were talking), but a pronoun must go inside: ✗ took aside me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of leading someone away for a private word. Progressive is fine — he's taking her aside now.
entries.passive: yes — I was taken aside after practice; the two students who had been whispering were taken aside.

entries.meaning: Remove something or someone; in arithmetic, subtract; and with from, reduce the effect of something.
examples: They took his license away for six months.
The waiter took our plates away before we finished.
Take it away — I can't look at it anymore.
Six take away two is four.
If you take away the tax, it's about forty dollars.
The loud music takes away from the food.
Nothing can take away from what she accomplished.
What I took away from the meeting was that nobody had a plan.
The main takeaway was that we need more time.

senses.head: Remove, confiscate, carry off
body: The everyday sense. The American noun for restaurant food eaten elsewhere is takeout; takeaway in that meaning is British. (забирать, уносить, отнимать)
examples: They took his license away for six months.
The waiter took our plates away before we finished.
Take it away — I can't look at it anymore.

senses.head: Subtract
body: Classroom arithmetic. Outside school an American says minus or subtract. (вычитать)
examples: Six take away two is four.
If you take away the tax, it's about forty dollars.

senses.head: Take away from — lessen
body: Three-part and inseparable: the thing diminished always follows from. (умалять, портить впечатление)
examples: The loud music takes away from the food.
Nothing can take away from what she accomplished.

senses.head: Take away from — come out with
body: What you leave an experience holding: a lesson, an impression. The noun takeaway comes from here. (вынести (урок, впечатление))
examples: What I took away from the meeting was that nobody had a plan.
The main takeaway was that we need more time.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — take away his phone or take his phone away, and a pronoun must split the phrase: take it away, never ✗ take away it. The three-part take away from is a different verb and never splits — nothing may come between away and from: the noise takes away from the meal, ✗ the noise takes the meal away from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the remove sense (they're taking his license away). The arithmetic sense is a frozen classroom formula that does not inflect — six take away two is four, ✗ six is taking away two — and take away from (lessen) is closer to stative.
entries.passive: restricted — full passive in the remove sense: his license was taken away for six months, our plates were taken away. None in the other senses: ✗ two is taken away from six, ✗ the food is taken away from by the loud music.
entries.see also: take back, take out, throw away

entries.meaning: Retract, return, readmit, or transport someone mentally to an earlier time.
examples: I take it back — you were right.
He refused to take back a single word of it.
She took the sweater back because it didn't fit.
You can take it back within thirty days with the receipt.
After everything, she still took him back.
The paper took her back two years later.
That song takes me back to high school.
The smell of chalk took her back thirty years.

senses.head: Retract what you said
body: Withdraw a statement, usually an unfair one. (брать слова обратно)
examples: I take it back — you were right.
He refused to take back a single word of it.

senses.head: Return a purchase
body: Bring something back to the store. (возвращать в магазин)
examples: She took the sweater back because it didn't fit.
You can take it back within thirty days with the receipt.

senses.head: Accept someone back
body: Let a partner or an employee return after a break. (принять обратно)
examples: After everything, she still took him back.
The paper took her back two years later.

senses.head: Bring the past vividly to mind
body: A smell or a song does this to you. (переносить в прошлое, навевать воспоминания)
examples: That song takes me back to high school.
The smell of chalk took her back thirty years.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: брать назад (слова); возвращать (покупку); принять обратно; переносить в прошлое
entries.separable: yes — take back the sweater or take the sweater back, and a pronoun must split: take it back, never ✗ take back it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: retracting, returning a purchase, readmitting a person, and (of a song or a smell) sending someone back in memory.
entries.passive: restricted — senses 1–3 passivize freely: the sweater was taken back, not one word of it was taken back, she was taken back two years later. The memory sense resists it: ✗ I am taken back to high school by that song.
entries.see also: take away, think back, win back

entries.meaning: Write something down, remove something from where it stands, or bring down a person or an organization.
examples: The officer took down my name and address.
Let me take that down before I forget it.
They took the tent down in the rain.
He took the posters down the day after the election.
Two agents took him down in the parking lot.
It took one whistleblower to take the company down.
Somebody needs to take him down a peg.
That loss took them down a notch.

senses.head: Write down what is said
body: Record details as you hear them. (записывать)
examples: The officer took down my name and address.
Let me take that down before I forget it.

senses.head: Remove or dismantle
body: Get something off a wall, or take a structure apart. (снимать, разбирать)
examples: They took the tent down in the rain.
He took the posters down the day after the election.

senses.head: Defeat, arrest, or destroy
body: Bring down someone powerful, or physically subdue a suspect. (свалить, задержать, покончить с)
examples: Two agents took him down in the parking lot.
It took one whistleblower to take the company down.

senses.head: Take down a peg
body: Deflate someone's self-importance. Also take down a notch. (сбить спесь)
examples: Somebody needs to take him down a peg.
That loss took them down a notch.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — take down the address or take the address down, and a pronoun must split: take it down, never ✗ take down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: writing down, dismantling, defeating or arresting, and the idiomatic take down a peg.
entries.passive: yes — my name and address were taken down; the tent was taken down in the rain; he was taken down in the parking lot; he needs to be taken down a peg.
entries.see also: take apart, tear down, write down

entries.meaning: Wrongly believe someone or something to be something else — and, in the fixed phrase take for granted, to stop noticing what you have.
examples: I took him for a security guard because of the jacket.
Everyone takes her for the boss.
Do you take me for an idiot?
What do you take us for?
He takes his wife for granted.
We took it for granted that the room would be free.

senses.head: Mistake one thing for another
body: Usually about identity or role. (принимать за)
examples: I took him for a security guard because of the jacket.
Everyone takes her for the boss.

senses.head: What do you take me for?
body: A challenge to someone's low opinion of you. (за кого ты меня принимаешь?)
examples: Do you take me for an idiot?
What do you take us for?

senses.head: Take for granted
body: Assume something without checking, or stop appreciating someone. (принимать как должное)
examples: He takes his wife for granted.
We took it for granted that the room would be free.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress; for is weak, usually /fɚ/
entries.type: prepositional verb (verb + preposition), with the object fixed in the middle
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — the object sits between take and for, and there is no joined order at all: I took him for a security guard, ✗ I took for him a security guard. A pronoun goes in the same slot and nowhere else: take it for granted, never ✗ take for granted it.
entries.verb type: stative — a judgment or a mistaken belief about identity, not an act, so the progressive is out: ✗ I am taking him for a security guard. The fixed take for granted is the same.
entries.passive: yes, unusually for a stative verb — he was taken for a security guard because of the jacket; it was taken for granted that the room would be free; she doesn't want to be taken for granted.

entries.meaning: Absorb, shelter, deceive, narrow, or go and see — one of the busiest phrasal verbs in the language.
examples: There was too much on the slide to take it all in.
She sat quietly, taking in everything that was said.
They took in two foster kids last spring.
A neighbor took us in after the fire.
Don't be taken in by the discount — it isn't one.
He took a lot of smart people in.
The tailor took the waist in two inches.
We took in a movie after dinner.
The tour takes in four cities in six days.

senses.head: Absorb and understand
body: Register information, or simply look at something at length. (усваивать, воспринимать)
examples: There was too much on the slide to take it all in.
She sat quietly, taking in everything that was said.

senses.head: Give shelter to
body: Let someone live with you. (приютить, взять к себе)
examples: They took in two foster kids last spring.
A neighbor took us in after the fire.

senses.head: Deceive
body: Usually passive: be taken in by. (обмануть, провести)
examples: Don't be taken in by the discount — it isn't one.
He took a lot of smart people in.

senses.head: Make a garment narrower
body: The tailor's sense; the opposite is let out. (ушить)
examples: The tailor took the waist in two inches.

senses.head: Go and see something
body: A movie, a game, a show. (сходить на, посмотреть)
examples: We took in a movie after dinner.
The tour takes in four cities in six days.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: понимать, усваивать; приютить; обмануть; ушить (одежду); сходить (на фильм)
entries.separable: yes — both orders work with a full noun, take in a movie or take a movie in, take in the waist or take the waist in, and a pronoun must split the phrase: take it in, never ✗ take in it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses: absorbing information (she sat taking it all in), sheltering, deceiving, narrowing a garment, and going to see a show.
entries.passive: yes — two foster kids were taken in last spring; the waist was taken in two inches. The deceive sense lives mostly in the passive: don't be taken in by the discount.
entries.see also: take on, take up, take for

entries.meaning: Remove something worn, leave the ground or the scene, suddenly succeed, or subtract time or money.
examples: Take your shoes off at the door.
She took off her coat and hung it by the door.
It's hot — take it off.
The plane took off forty minutes late.
He took off down the alley before anyone could stop him.
The business really took off after the article ran.
I'm taking Friday off.
She took off three days to move.
The manager took ten dollars off the bill.
In Britain they'd say she takes the boss off perfectly; in the US we'd say she does a great impression of him.

senses.head: Remove something worn or attached
body: Clothes, glasses, a lid, a label. (снимать)
examples: Take your shoes off at the door.
She took off her coat and hung it by the door.
It's hot — take it off.

senses.head: Leave the ground
body: Of aircraft; the noun is takeoff. (взлетать)
examples: The plane took off forty minutes late.

senses.head: Leave suddenly
body: Informal: go, fast, often without explaining. (сорваться, умчаться)
examples: He took off down the alley before anyone could stop him.

senses.head: Suddenly succeed
body: Of a product, a career, an idea. (пойти в гору, набрать популярность)
examples: The business really took off after the article ran.

senses.head: Take time off; deduct
body: Not work for a stretch, or knock money off a price. (взять отгул; скинуть, вычесть)
examples: I'm taking Friday off.
She took off three days to move.
The manager took ten dollars off the bill.

senses.head: Imitate mockingly
body: British. Americans say do an impression of. (пародировать)
examples: In Britain they'd say she takes the boss off perfectly; in the US we'd say she does a great impression of him.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: снимать (одежду); взлетать; сорваться и уйти; пойти в гору; взять отгул
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — take off your coat or take your coat off, and a pronoun must split: take it off, never ✗ take off it. In the intransitive senses (a plane, a business) there is no object to place.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you remove something or deduct time, intransitive when a plane or a business takes off
entries.verb type: action — dynamic everywhere: removing something worn, leaving the ground, bolting, suddenly succeeding, and deducting time or money.
entries.passive: restricted — the transitive senses passivize: shoes must be taken off at the door, ten dollars was taken off the bill. The intransitive senses have no passive at all: ✗ it was taken off by the plane, ✗ the business was taken off.
entries.see also: take on, take out, throw on

entries.meaning: Accept work, hire someone, acquire a quality, or square up to an opponent bigger than you.
examples: She took on three new clients this month.
Don't take any more on — you're already buried.
The warehouse is taking on seasonal workers.
They took him on as an apprentice.
His voice took on an edge I hadn't heard before.
The whole story takes on a different meaning once you know that.
A small firm took on the state and won.
Nobody wanted to take them on in court.

senses.head: Accept work or responsibility
body: Agree to carry something. (браться за, брать на себя)
examples: She took on three new clients this month.
Don't take any more on — you're already buried.

senses.head: Hire
body: Add someone to a payroll. (нанимать)
examples: The warehouse is taking on seasonal workers.
They took him on as an apprentice.

senses.head: Acquire a quality
body: Of a voice, a story, a color: come to have it. (приобретать (черты, оттенок))
examples: His voice took on an edge I hadn't heard before.
The whole story takes on a different meaning once you know that.

senses.head: Fight or compete with
body: Especially against a stronger side. (сразиться с, бросить вызов)
examples: A small firm took on the state and won.
Nobody wanted to take them on in court.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: браться за, взваливать на себя; нанимать; приобретать (черты); сразиться с
entries.separable: yes — take on more work or take more work on, and a pronoun must split: take it on, never ✗ take on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the accept-work, hire, and fight senses. Sense 3 (his voice took on an edge) is an inchoative change of state — still dynamic, but with an inanimate, non-agentive subject.
entries.passive: restricted — the agentive senses passivize: three new clients were taken on, he was taken on as an apprentice, the state was taken on and beaten. Sense 3 does not: ✗ an edge was taken on by his voice.
entries.see also: take up, take over, thrust upon

entries.meaning: Remove something, escort someone out for an evening, obtain something official, or destroy a target.
examples: He took the trash out before dinner.
Take the batteries out if you're storing it.
She took me out for my birthday.
He's taking her out on Friday.
They took out a loan against the house.
We took out a full-page ad in the paper.
One missile took out the bridge.
The flu took half the office out for a week.
We ordered Chinese takeout and ate it on the floor.

senses.head: Remove from a place
body: The literal core. (вынимать, доставать)
examples: He took the trash out before dinner.
Take the batteries out if you're storing it.

senses.head: Escort someone out and pay
body: Dinner, a movie, a birthday. (пригласить, сводить куда-то)
examples: She took me out for my birthday.
He's taking her out on Friday.

senses.head: Obtain something official
body: A loan, an insurance policy, an ad, a permit. (оформить, взять (кредит), поместить (объявление))
examples: They took out a loan against the house.
We took out a full-page ad in the paper.

senses.head: Destroy or disable
body: Informal and military: kill, knock out, put out of action. (устранить, вывести из строя)
examples: One missile took out the bridge.
The flu took half the office out for a week.

senses.head: Food to eat elsewhere
body: The American noun is takeout; Britain says takeaway. (еда навынос)
examples: We ordered Chinese takeout and ate it on the floor.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: вынимать; пригласить куда-то; оформить (кредит, страховку); устранить
entries.separable: yes — take out the trash or take the trash out, and a pronoun must split: take it out, never ✗ take out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four verbal senses: removing, escorting someone out, obtaining something official, and destroying a target. (Takeout, the food, is a noun.)
entries.passive: yes in every sense — the trash was taken out before dinner; I was taken out for my birthday; a loan was taken out against the house; the bridge was taken out by one missile.
entries.see also: take out on, take in, throw out

entries.meaning: Vent anger or frustration on someone who did nothing to cause it.
examples: Don't take it out on the kids.
She took her bad day out on everybody in the office.
I'm sorry — I took my frustration out on you.
He takes everything out on whoever happens to be closest.
Whatever happened at work, don't take it out on me.
entries.pronunciation note: the first particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun obligatorily so — the feeling sits between take and out and the person follows on: take your anger out on me, take it out on me. A pronoun can go nowhere else: ✗ take out it on me. With a full noun the unsplit order is heard too: take out your frustration on the kids. Nothing may ever come between out and on: ✗ take it out today on me.
entries.transitive: yes — two objects, one before out and one after on
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: an act of venting, and progressive is normal — you're taking it out on the kids again.
entries.passive: restricted — the feeling can be promoted: his frustration was taken out on whoever was closest. The person after on cannot: ✗ the kids were taken it out on, ✗ I was taken out on.
entries.see also: take out, tell off, tear into

entries.meaning: Assume control of something from whoever had it.
examples: Can you take over for an hour? I need a break.
She took the class over when the teacher quit.
A bigger firm took us over last year.
Rebels took over the airport before dawn.
Panic took over and people ran for the doors.
Once the vines started, they took the whole yard over.

senses.head: Assume a duty from someone else
body: Step into the job while the other person steps out. (принять на себя, сменить кого-то)
examples: Can you take over for an hour? I need a break.
She took the class over when the teacher quit.

senses.head: Gain control of a company or a place
body: The noun is takeover. (захватить, поглотить)
examples: A bigger firm took us over last year.
Rebels took over the airport before dawn.

senses.head: Become dominant
body: Of a feeling, a species, a habit. (взять верх, заполонить)
examples: Panic took over and people ran for the doors.
Once the vines started, they took the whole yard over.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: взять на себя, принять руководство; захватить; поглотить (компанию)
entries.separable: yes — take over the class or take the class over, and a pronoun must split: take it over, never ✗ take over it. With no object at all it stays whole: can you take over for an hour?
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you name what is taken, intransitive in take over for someone
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: assuming a duty, seizing a company or a place, or (of panic, vines, a habit) becoming dominant.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the class was taken over when the teacher quit; we were taken over by a bigger firm; the airport was taken over before dawn. The intransitive take over for someone has no passive.
entries.see also: take on, take up, wind down

entries.meaning: Start liking something quickly, fall into a habit, or head for a place.
examples: The baby took to her new nanny right away.
I never really took to the city.
He has taken to getting up at five.
She took to running after the surgery.
Thousands took to the streets that night.
They took to the hills when the flooding started.

senses.head: Start liking quickly
body: Warm to a person or a thing right away. (проникнуться, полюбить сразу)
examples: The baby took to her new nanny right away.
I never really took to the city.

senses.head: Fall into a habit
body: Followed by an -ing form. (пристраститься, взять в привычку)
examples: He has taken to getting up at five.
She took to running after the surgery.

senses.head: Head for a place
body: Usually for shelter, escape, or protest. (податься, укрыться в, выйти на)
examples: Thousands took to the streets that night.
They took to the hills when the flooding started.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: проникнуться симпатией к; пристраститься к; податься, удариться в
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: took to her right away, took to it right away. ✗ took her to, ✗ took it to in this meaning.
entries.verb type: action — inceptive rather than fully dynamic: it names the moment liking or a habit begins, which is why the progressive is odd (✗ she is taking to the new nanny) while has taken to getting up at five is normal. Sense 3, heading for a place, is plainly dynamic.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional object stays put in all three senses: ✗ the new nanny was taken to right away, ✗ running was taken to after the surgery, ✗ the streets were taken to that night.

entries.meaning: Begin an activity, occupy space or time, resume something, or shorten a garment.
examples: She took up the guitar at forty.
He took woodworking up after he retired.
That couch takes up half the room.
Sorry to take up so much of your time.
Let's take it up where we stopped yesterday.
She took up the story again after the interruption.
If you don't like the policy, take it up with HR.
The tailor took the hem up an inch.

senses.head: Start a hobby or activity
body: Begin doing something new on a regular basis. (заняться, начать заниматься)
examples: She took up the guitar at forty.
He took woodworking up after he retired.

senses.head: Occupy space or time
body: Fill it, usually more than you wanted. (занимать (место, время))
examples: That couch takes up half the room.
Sorry to take up so much of your time.

senses.head: Resume
body: Continue from where something stopped. (продолжить, подхватить)
examples: Let's take it up where we stopped yesterday.
She took up the story again after the interruption.

senses.head: Take up with — raise a matter
body: Bring an issue to the person who can act on it. Not to be confused with the entry take up with. (поднять вопрос, обратиться с)
examples: If you don't like the policy, take it up with HR.

senses.head: Shorten a garment
body: The tailor's sense; the opposite is let down. (подшить, укоротить)
examples: The tailor took the hem up an inch.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: заняться (чем-то новым); занимать (место, время); продолжить; подшить
entries.separable: yes — take up the guitar or take the guitar up, and a pronoun must split: take it up, never ✗ take up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the start-a-hobby, resume, raise-a-matter, and tailoring senses. The occupy-space sense is closer to stative: that couch takes up half the room describes a state, not an event.
entries.passive: yes — half the room is taken up by that couch; the hem was taken up an inch; the story was taken up again after the interruption; it should be taken up with HR.
entries.see also: take up on, take up with, take on

entries.meaning: Accept an offer or invitation someone has made, sometimes with a hint of holding them to their word.
examples: I might take you up on that.
She took him up on his offer of a ride.
If the room is really free, we'll take you up on it.
He took them up on the challenge and won.
Nobody ever took her up on the invitation.
entries.pronunciation note: the first particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — the person goes between take and up, noun or pronoun alike, and the offer follows on: take you up on it, take the neighbors up on their offer. ✗ take up you on it, ✗ take up the neighbors on their offer. Nothing separates up from on.
entries.transitive: yes — the person before on, the offer after it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of accepting an offer. Progressive is fine — I'm taking you up on that.
entries.passive: restricted — the person passivizes naturally: she was taken up on her offer of a ride; nobody was ever taken up on that invitation. The offer after on cannot move: ✗ the offer was taken her up on.

entries.meaning: Begin spending time with someone, almost always someone the speaker disapproves of. Slightly dated, and never neutral.
examples: He took up with a rough crowd his senior year.
She took up with somebody she met online.
After the divorce he took up with an old classmate.
Her parents hated that she'd taken up with him.
They took up with a group of street musicians for the summer.
entries.pronunciation note: the first particle carries the stress
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: took up with a rough crowd, took up with them. ✗ took a rough crowd up with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: beginning to keep company with someone. Progressive is possible but rare — she's been taking up with the wrong people.
entries.passive: no — the object of with resists promotion: ✗ a rough crowd was taken up with by him, ✗ he was taken up with after the divorce.
entries.see also: take up, take to, throw over

entries.meaning: Rip something to pieces, or do the emotional equivalent to a person, a family, or a town.
examples: The dog tore the cushion apart.
The storm tore apart three barns on that road.
It tore her apart to leave him behind.
The scandal tore the town apart.
They tore the apartment apart looking for the passport.
Don't tear it apart just to see how it works.

senses.head: Rip or pull to pieces
body: Physical destruction, by hands, animals, or weather. (разорвать, разнести)
examples: The dog tore the cushion apart.
The storm tore apart three barns on that road.

senses.head: Divide people, or distress someone deeply
body: Of grief, scandal, or conflict. (разрывать, раздирать)
examples: It tore her apart to leave him behind.
The scandal tore the town apart.

senses.head: Search a place violently
body: Turn everything over looking for something. (перерыть всё, перевернуть вверх дном)
examples: They tore the apartment apart looking for the passport.
Don't tear it apart just to see how it works.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: разорвать на части; разрывать (душу); перевернуть всё вверх дном
entries.separable: yes — tear apart the cushion or tear the cushion apart, and a pronoun must split: tear it apart, never ✗ tear apart it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: ripping to pieces, dividing or distressing people, and ransacking a place.
entries.passive: yes — the cushion was torn apart by the dog; the town was torn apart by the scandal; the apartment was torn apart looking for the passport.
entries.see also: take apart, tear up, tear down

entries.meaning: Pull violently and repeatedly at something — or, of guilt and grief, at someone.
examples: He tore at the packaging with his teeth.
The wind tore at the tarp all night.
She tore at the knot until her fingers bled.
The guilt tore at him for years.
It tears at me every time I think about it.

senses.head: Pull violently at something
body: Repeated action, often unsuccessful. (рвать, драть, царапать)
examples: He tore at the packaging with his teeth.
The wind tore at the tarp all night.
She tore at the knot until her fingers bled.

senses.head: Cause lasting distress
body: Of a feeling that keeps working on you. (терзать, разрывать сердце)
examples: The guilt tore at him for years.
It tears at me every time I think about it.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: tore at the wrapping, tore at it. ✗ tore the wrapping at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and durative in both senses: repeated pulling (she was tearing at the knot) and guilt that keeps working on someone (it tears at me).
entries.passive: restricted, and marginal at best — a prepositional passive is barely possible for the physical sense: ?the wrapping had been torn at. The distress sense has none: ✗ he was torn at by guilt for years.

entries.meaning: Force someone — usually yourself — to leave something absorbing; or pull something off by force.
examples: I couldn't tear myself away from the game.
She finally tore herself away at midnight.
Can you tear yourself away for five minutes?
He tore the kids away from the screen for dinner.
She tore away the plastic film and plugged it in.

senses.head: Force yourself or someone to leave
body: The everyday sense, nearly always reflexive. (оторвать(ся))
examples: I couldn't tear myself away from the game.
She finally tore herself away at midnight.
Can you tear yourself away for five minutes?
He tore the kids away from the screen for dinner.

senses.head: Pull off forcibly
body: Physical removal, usually of something stuck on. (сорвать, содрать)
examples: She tore away the plastic film and plugged it in.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — with a full noun either order works, tear away the plastic film or tear the plastic film away, and in the common reflexive use the object is always inside: tear yourself away, tear him away, never ✗ tear away yourself, ✗ tear away him.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object, very often a reflexive pronoun
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing someone (usually yourself) to leave something absorbing, or ripping something off by force.
entries.passive: restricted — fine when someone else does it: the kids were torn away from the screen; the plastic film was torn away. The reflexive use, which is the common one, has no passive: ✗ myself was torn away from the game.

entries.meaning: Demolish a building, dismantle a rig, or attack someone's reputation.
examples: They tore down the old high school in June.
The city tore it down without warning.
He tears other people down to feel bigger.
It's easier to tear something down than to build it.
The crew tore the stage down in under two hours.

senses.head: Demolish
body: The core sense; the opposite of put up. (сносить)
examples: They tore down the old high school in June.
The city tore it down without warning.

senses.head: Attack someone's reputation
body: Belittle a person instead of building them up. (очернять, поносить)
examples: He tears other people down to feel bigger.
It's easier to tear something down than to build it.

senses.head: Dismantle equipment
body: Strike a stage, break down a rig. (разбирать, демонтировать)
examples: The crew tore the stage down in under two hours.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — tear down the school or tear the school down, and a pronoun must split: tear it down, never ✗ tear down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: demolishing, belittling a person, and striking a stage or rig.
entries.passive: yes — the old high school was torn down in June; the stage was torn down in under two hours; nobody likes being torn down in public.
entries.see also: tear apart, take down, tear out

entries.meaning: Attack something or someone with sudden energy — with words, teeth, or effort.
examples: She tore into him in front of the whole staff.
The coach tore into the team at halftime.
He tore into the sandwich like he hadn't eaten in days.
The kids tore into their presents before breakfast.
They tore into the work and had it done by noon.

senses.head: Criticize fiercely
body: A verbal assault, usually public. (наброситься на, разнести)
examples: She tore into him in front of the whole staff.
The coach tore into the team at halftime.

senses.head: Start on something with great energy
body: Food, presents, work. (накинуться на, взяться с жаром)
examples: He tore into the sandwich like he hadn't eaten in days.
The kids tore into their presents before breakfast.
They tore into the work and had it done by noon.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: наброситься с критикой на; накинуться на (еду, работу)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: tore into him, tore into it. ✗ tore him into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a sudden burst of energy aimed at a person, a plate of food, or a job. Progressive is normal — he's tearing into the sandwich.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is awkward even in the criticize sense: ?he was torn into in front of the whole staff. The energy sense refuses it: ✗ the presents were torn into by the kids.
entries.see also: tear at, tell off, tear through

entries.meaning: Remove something by tearing, pull clothing off in a hurry, or leave at speed.
examples: Tear off the bottom of the form and mail it in.
He tore the receipt off and handed it to me.
Don't tear it off — you'll need the stub.
He tore off his wet jacket and threw it in the corner.
She tore off down the driveway without saying goodbye.

senses.head: Remove by tearing
body: A coupon, a stub, a strip. (оторвать)
examples: Tear off the bottom of the form and mail it in.
He tore the receipt off and handed it to me.
Don't tear it off — you'll need the stub.

senses.head: Pull clothing off fast
body: Impatient removal. (сорвать с себя)
examples: He tore off his wet jacket and threw it in the corner.

senses.head: Leave in a hurry
body: Informal, intransitive. (умчаться, сорваться)
examples: She tore off down the driveway without saying goodbye.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: оторвать; сорвать с себя; умчаться, сорваться с места
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — tear off the stub or tear the stub off, and a pronoun must split: tear it off, never ✗ tear off it. In the "leave fast" sense there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you rip something off, intransitive when you leave in a hurry
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping something free, pulling clothing off fast, or (intransitively) leaving at speed.
entries.passive: restricted — the transitive senses passivize: the stub was torn off and mailed in; his wet jacket was torn off. The leave-fast sense is intransitive and has none: ✗ the driveway was torn off down.
entries.see also: tear out, tear up, take off

entries.meaning: Rip something out of the thing it was fixed in, or leave a place very fast.
examples: She tore out the page and put it in her pocket.
Somebody tore three pages out of the manual.
Tear it out and start over.
They tore out the carpet and found hardwood underneath.
He tore out of the parking lot doing forty.

senses.head: Remove by tearing
body: A page, a coupon, a photo. (вырвать, выдрать)
examples: She tore out the page and put it in her pocket.
Somebody tore three pages out of the manual.
Tear it out and start over.

senses.head: Rip out and replace
body: Construction: strip a surface down to the frame. (содрать, демонтировать)
examples: They tore out the carpet and found hardwood underneath.

senses.head: Leave very fast
body: Informal, intransitive. (вылететь, рвануть)
examples: He tore out of the parking lot doing forty.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — tear out the page or tear the page out, and a pronoun must split: tear it out, never ✗ tear out it. The "leave fast" sense takes no object.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you rip something out, intransitive when you leave at speed
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping something out of what held it, stripping a surface, or (intransitively) leaving very fast.
entries.passive: restricted — the transitive senses passivize: three pages had been torn out of the manual; the carpet was torn out and hardwood was found underneath. The leave-fast sense has no object and no passive.
entries.see also: tear off, tear down, tear up

entries.meaning: Move through something violently and fast, or get through it far quicker than expected.
examples: The fire tore through four buildings before dawn.
A truck tore through the fence and into the field.
He tore through the first three chapters in one sitting.
The kids tore through two pizzas in ten minutes.
She tore through her savings in under a year.

senses.head: Move through violently
body: Fire, storms, vehicles. (пронестись, промчаться сквозь)
examples: The fire tore through four buildings before dawn.
A truck tore through the fence and into the field.

senses.head: Get through quickly
body: Books, food, money, work. (проглотить, спустить, разделаться с)
examples: He tore through the first three chapters in one sitting.
The kids tore through two pizzas in ten minutes.
She tore through her savings in under a year.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: пронестись сквозь; быстро разделаться с, спустить (деньги)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: tore through four buildings, tore through them. ✗ tore four buildings through.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: moving through something violently (the fire tore through four buildings) and getting through it fast (she tore through her savings).
entries.passive: no — the prepositional object cannot be promoted in either sense: ✗ four buildings were torn through by the fire, ✗ two pizzas were torn through in ten minutes.

entries.meaning: Destroy something by ripping it, cancel an agreement, or chew up a surface. A fourth sense is a different verb entirely.
examples: He tore up the letter without reading it.
She tore the check up in front of him.
Tear it up and we'll print another one.
The company tore up the contract in March.
The plows tore up the lawn along the curb.
He teared up when they played the song.

senses.head: Destroy by ripping
body: Paper, mostly. (порвать, разорвать)
examples: He tore up the letter without reading it.
She tore the check up in front of him.
Tear it up and we'll print another one.

senses.head: Cancel an agreement
body: Figurative: refuse to be bound by it. (разорвать, аннулировать)
examples: The company tore up the contract in March.

senses.head: Damage a surface
body: Roads, lawns, turf. (разворотить, разбить)
examples: The plows tore up the lawn along the curb.

senses.head: Eyes fill with tears
body: A trap: this is a different verb, from the noun tear /tɪr/, and it is regular — teared up, /tɪrd/, not tore up. (прослезиться)
examples: He teared up when they played the song.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: порвать в клочья; расторгнуть (договор); разворотить; прослезиться
entries.separable: yes — tear up the letter or tear the letter up, and a pronoun must split: tear it up, never ✗ tear up it. Sense 4 takes no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when you rip something up, intransitive when someone's eyes tear up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping paper, canceling an agreement, chewing up a surface. Sense 4 is a different, regular verb (teared up, from the noun tear /tɪr/) and is an intransitive change of state.
entries.passive: restricted — the three transitive senses passivize: the letter was torn up without being read; the contract was torn up in March; the lawn was torn up by the plows. The eyes sense cannot: ✗ he was teared up.
entries.see also: tear apart, tear off, write off

entries.meaning: Distinguish two or more very similar things from each other. It appears mostly in the negative or with can.
examples: I can't tell the twins apart.
Nobody can tell them apart over the phone.
Can you tell the two recordings apart?
After a while you learn to tell the calls apart.
The copies are so good that experts can't tell them apart.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes, and in practice the object nearly always sits inside: tell the twins apart. With a pronoun it must: tell them apart, never ✗ tell apart them.
entries.verb type: stative — an ability to perceive a difference, not an act, which is why it lives under can and the negative and rejects the progressive: ✗ I am telling the twins apart.
entries.passive: yes, though almost always under a modal — the twins can't be told apart over the phone; the copies are so good that they can't be told apart by experts.

entries.meaning: Scold someone angrily and to their face.
examples: She told him off in front of everybody.
I finally told the guy off.
He got told off for showing up late again.
Don't tell me off — I wasn't even there.
My mother told off the whole soccer team.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — tell off the whole team or tell the whole team off, and a pronoun must split: tell him off, never ✗ tell off him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of scolding someone to their face. Progressive is fine — she was telling him off in front of everybody.
entries.passive: yes, and the informal get-passive is very common — he got told off for showing up late again; I was told off in front of the whole staff.
entries.see also: tear into, take down, tell on

entries.meaning: Report someone's wrongdoing — or, of strain and age, start to show on someone.
examples: He told on me for eating the cookies.
Nobody wants to be the kid who tells on their friends.
She threatened to tell on him.
The late nights are starting to tell on her.
Twenty years of construction work told on his knees.

senses.head: Report someone's wrongdoing
body: Informal, and mostly children's talk; adults say report or turn in. (наябедничать, донести)
examples: He told on me for eating the cookies.
Nobody wants to be the kid who tells on their friends.
She threatened to tell on him.

senses.head: Show a visible effect on someone
body: Of long hours, hard work, or years. (сказываться на, давать о себе знать)
examples: The late nights are starting to tell on her.
Twenty years of construction work told on his knees.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: наябедничать на, донести на; сказываться на
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: told on his brother, told on him. ✗ told his brother on, ✗ told him on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the informing sense (he's telling on me again). The show-an-effect sense is gradual and closer to stative: the late nights are starting to tell on her.
entries.passive: restricted — the informal get-passive is heard in the schoolyard sense: I got told on; the be-passive is stiffer: ?he was told on by his sister. The show-an-effect sense has none: ✗ his knees were told on by twenty years of construction work.

entries.meaning: Cast your mind back to an earlier time.
examples: Think back to the first day you started here.
When I think back, none of it made sense.
She thought back on the whole conversation.
Thinking back, I should have said no.
He thinks back to that trip more often than he admits.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. What you remember follows on or to: think back on that summer, think back to 1998.
entries.transitive: no, never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a deliberate mental act, and the progressive is normal — thinking back, I should have said no.
entries.passive: no — there is no direct object at all, and what is remembered sits behind to or on and cannot be promoted: ✗ that summer was thought back on, ✗ 1998 was thought back to.

entries.meaning: Hold an opinion, come up with an idea, recall something, or consider doing something.
examples: What do you think of the new place?
He thinks very highly of your work.
They don't think much of the new policy.
Who thought of putting the sink there?
I can't think of her last name.
We're thinking of moving in the spring.

senses.head: Have an opinion about
body: The standard way to ask for a reaction. (быть какого-то мнения)
examples: What do you think of the new place?
He thinks very highly of your work.
They don't think much of the new policy.

senses.head: Come up with an idea
body: Invent or propose. (придумать)
examples: Who thought of putting the sink there?

senses.head: Recall
body: Retrieve something from memory, usually with difficulty. (вспомнить)
examples: I can't think of her last name.

senses.head: Consider doing
body: Followed by an -ing form. (подумывать о)
examples: We're thinking of moving in the spring.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: думать о; придумать; вспомнить; быть какого-то мнения о
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: thought of a name, thought of it. ✗ thought a name of. The only thing that ever comes between is an adverb of degree: think highly of her.
entries.verb type: stative in the opinion sense — a held attitude, not an act: ✗ he is thinking highly of your work. Dynamic in the come-up-with, recall, and consider senses: we're thinking of moving in the spring.
entries.passive: restricted — the opinion sense passivizes in fixed formulas: she is very highly thought of, the new policy isn't much thought of. The other senses barely do: ?who was that idea thought of by, ✗ her last name couldn't be thought of.
entries.see also: think up, think over, think back

entries.meaning: Work something out fully in advance, down to the details. You will meet it most often as the participle well thought out.
examples: The plan wasn't thought out at all.
She thought the whole thing out before she said a word.
Think it out first, then start writing.
He thought out every objection they might raise.
It was a beautifully thought-out answer.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — think out the whole plan or think the whole plan out, and a pronoun must split: think it out, never ✗ think out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: working a plan through to its details in advance. Progressive is possible but uncommon — he's still thinking it out.
entries.passive: yes, and the participle is where you usually meet it — the plan wasn't thought out at all; it was a beautifully thought-out answer.

entries.meaning: Consider something carefully before deciding.
examples: Think it over and call me tomorrow.
She wanted a week to think over the offer.
I thought the whole thing over on the drive home.
Don't answer now — think it over.
He thought over what she'd said and changed his mind.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — think over the offer or think the offer over, and a pronoun must split: think it over, never ✗ think over it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: deliberating before deciding. Progressive is fine — I'm still thinking it over.
entries.passive: yes, though the active is far more common — the offer was thought over for a week before she answered; it deserves to be thought over carefully.

entries.meaning: Follow an idea all the way to its consequences before acting on it.
examples: You haven't thought this through.
Let's think through what happens if the funding falls apart.
She thought it through and decided not to sign.
Think the whole sequence through one more time.
Nobody thought through the cost of maintaining it.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — think through the consequences or think the consequences through, and a pronoun must split: think it through, never ✗ think through it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: following an idea out to its consequences. Progressive is fine — we're thinking through what happens if the funding falls apart.
entries.passive: yes — this hasn't been thought through; the cost of maintaining it was never thought through.

entries.meaning: Invent something on the spot — an excuse, a plan, a name.
examples: He thought up a reason to leave early.
She thought the whole scheme up in an afternoon.
Who thought that up?
I couldn't think up a good excuse fast enough.
They thought up a name for the band on the way to the show.
Don't ask me how she thought it up.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — think up an excuse or think an excuse up, and a pronoun must split: think it up, never ✗ think up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: a single act of invention, fine in the progressive (he's still thinking up excuses).
entries.passive: yes, though the active is far more common — the whole scheme was thought up in an afternoon, that name was thought up on the way to the show.

entries.meaning: Get rid of something, or waste an advantage you already had.
examples: Don't throw that away — I need the box.
He threw away everything in the fridge.
Throw it away, it's past the date.
She threw away a two-goal lead in ten minutes.
He threw his career away over a stupid argument.
He threw the best line in the movie away like it was nothing.
Don't throw it away — that line deserves a pause.
It was a throwaway remark, but it stuck with me.

senses.head: Discard
body: Put in the trash. (выбрасывать)
examples: Don't throw that away — I need the box.
He threw away everything in the fridge.
Throw it away, it's past the date.

senses.head: Waste an opportunity
body: Lose through carelessness what you were holding. (упустить, растратить впустую)
examples: She threw away a two-goal lead in ten minutes.
He threw his career away over a stupid argument.

senses.head: Deliver a line casually
body: Toss a remark out as though it did not matter — the adjective throwaway comes from here. (бросить вскользь)
examples: He threw the best line in the movie away like it was nothing.
Don't throw it away — that line deserves a pause.
It was a throwaway remark, but it stuck with me.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — throw away the box or throw the box away, and a pronoun must split: throw it away, never ✗ throw away it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: discarding, squandering a lead, and tossing off a line are all things done.
entries.passive: yes — the box was thrown away, a two-goal lead was thrown away in ten minutes. The participle also hardens into the adjective a throwaway remark.
entries.see also: throw out, take away, write off

entries.meaning: Return a fish to the water, repel an attack, set progress back, or leave someone with only their last resort.
examples: It was under the limit, so he threw it back.
They threw back two more before the rain started.
Our troops threw the attack back at the ridge.
The delay threw us back almost two months.
With the internet down, we were thrown back on paper files.

senses.head: Return a caught fish
body: Angling. (отпустить обратно)
examples: It was under the limit, so he threw it back.
They threw back two more before the rain started.

senses.head: Repel an attack
body: Military. (отбросить, отбить)
examples: Our troops threw the attack back at the ridge.

senses.head: Set back
body: Delay progress by a measurable amount. (отбросить назад)
examples: The delay threw us back almost two months.

senses.head: Be thrown back on
body: Be left with nothing but a fallback. (быть вынужденным полагаться на)
examples: With the internet down, we were thrown back on paper files.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: отпустить обратно (рыбу); отбросить (противника); задержать; (be thrown back on) быть вынужденным полагаться на
entries.separable: yes — throw back the fish or throw the fish back, and a pronoun must split: throw it back, never ✗ throw back it. The passive three-part be thrown back on never splits.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from returning a fish to delaying a schedule.
entries.passive: yes — the fish was thrown back, the attack was thrown back at the ridge. Sense 4 exists only as a passive: we were thrown back on paper files, never ✗ the outage threw us back on paper files in that fixed shape.

entries.meaning: Add something extra — to a deal or to a conversation.
examples: They threw in free shipping.
He threw a set of floor mats in to close the deal.
If you buy two, they'll throw one in.
Ask about the roof rack — they'll probably throw it in.
She threw in a comment about the budget and the room went quiet.
After the third rejection he threw in the towel.
Two of the smaller unions threw in with the strikers.

senses.head: Add at no charge
body: Sweeten a deal. (добавить в придачу)
examples: They threw in free shipping.
He threw a set of floor mats in to close the deal.
If you buy two, they'll throw one in.
Ask about the roof rack — they'll probably throw it in.

senses.head: Add a remark
body: Drop a comment into a conversation. (вставить реплику)
examples: She threw in a comment about the budget and the room went quiet.

senses.head: Throw in the towel
body: Give up. From boxing, where the corner really does throw a towel. (сдаться)
examples: After the third rejection he threw in the towel.

senses.head: Throw in with
body: Join forces with someone. (примкнуть к)
examples: Two of the smaller unions threw in with the strikers.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: добавить в придачу; вставить (реплику); throw in the towel — сдаться
entries.separable: yes — throw in free shipping or throw free shipping in, and a pronoun must split: throw it in, never ✗ throw in it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: adding a freebie or dropping a remark into a conversation.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the freebie and remark senses (free shipping was thrown in, a comment about the budget was thrown in), but the idioms refuse: ✗ the towel was thrown in, and throw in with has no passive at all.
entries.see also: throw out, throw together, weave in

entries.meaning: Disconcert someone, shake off something that is following or afflicting you, or give off heat and light.
examples: The change in schedule threw me off.
Her accent threw us off at first.
Don't let the name throw you off — it's the same product.
They threw off the dogs by wading up the creek.
He couldn't throw off the cold for three weeks.
She threw off her coat and got to work.
The old radiator throws off a lot of heat.

senses.head: Confuse or disconcert
body: Knock someone's bearings out from under them. (сбить с толку, выбить из колеи)
examples: The change in schedule threw me off.
Her accent threw us off at first.
Don't let the name throw you off — it's the same product.

senses.head: Shake off a pursuer or an illness
body: Get free of something that is on you. (стряхнуть, отделаться от)
examples: They threw off the dogs by wading up the creek.
He couldn't throw off the cold for three weeks.

senses.head: Remove clothing quickly
body: Impatient removal. (сбросить)
examples: She threw off her coat and got to work.

senses.head: Emit
body: Heat, light, sparks, a smell. (испускать, выделять)
examples: The old radiator throws off a lot of heat.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: сбить с толку; стряхнуть, отделаться от; сбросить (одежду); испускать
entries.separable: yes — throw off the dogs or throw the dogs off, and a pronoun must split: throw me off, never ✗ throw off me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses; even the emit sense (the radiator throws off heat) reports ongoing activity, not a state.
entries.passive: yes — I was thrown off by the change in schedule, the dogs were thrown off at the creek, a lot of heat is thrown off by that old radiator.
entries.see also: take aback, throw out, put off

entries.meaning: Put clothes on quickly and without care — and, by extension, put music or coffee on the same way.
examples: Let me throw on a sweater.
He threw a jacket on and ran outside.
Throw it on — nobody's going to notice.
She threw on some music while she cooked.
I'll throw a pot of coffee on.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — throw on a sweater or throw a sweater on, and a pronoun must split: throw it on, never ✗ throw on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and the hurry is part of the meaning: clothes, music, or coffee put on fast.
entries.passive: restricted — the agentless passive is fine (a jacket was thrown on over pajamas), but naming the agent sounds wrong: ✗ a sweater was thrown on by her.
entries.see also: take off, throw off, throw together

entries.meaning: Discard something, eject someone, reject a case, float an idea, or wreck your back.
examples: Throw those out — they're moldy.
She threw out half of what was in the closet.
They threw him out after the second warning.
The judge threw the case out.
Let me just throw an idea out here.
He threw his back out lifting the couch.

senses.head: Discard
body: Same as throw away. (выбрасывать)
examples: Throw those out — they're moldy.
She threw out half of what was in the closet.

senses.head: Eject someone
body: Remove a person from a place or an organization. (выгнать, вышвырнуть)
examples: They threw him out after the second warning.

senses.head: Reject formally
body: Of a court or a committee. (отклонить, отменить)
examples: The judge threw the case out.

senses.head: Float an idea
body: Offer a suggestion for others to react to. (подкинуть, вбросить идею)
examples: Let me just throw an idea out here.

senses.head: Injure by sudden strain
body: Almost always a back. (потянуть, сорвать спину)
examples: He threw his back out lifting the couch.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — throw out the leftovers or throw the leftovers out, and a pronoun must split: throw them out, never ✗ throw out them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses: discarding, ejecting, rejecting, floating an idea, wrenching your back.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1–4 — the leftovers were thrown out, he was thrown out after the second warning, the case was thrown out by the judge. Sense 5 resists an agent: ✗ his back was thrown out by him, though my back got thrown out is idiomatic.
entries.see also: throw away, take out, throw in

entries.meaning: Abandon a partner or an ally, usually for someone better placed. Dated: you will meet it in novels far more often than in speech.
examples: She threw him over for a man with money.
He was thrown over the week before the wedding.
They say she threw over a perfectly good fiancé.
Don't throw her over on a whim.
He threw over his old friends the moment he got famous.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — throw over her fiancé or throw her fiancé over, and a pronoun must split: threw him over, never ✗ threw over him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and dated: abandoning a partner or an ally, mostly a novelist's verb now.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commoner shape — he was thrown over the week before the wedding.

entries.meaning: Assemble something quickly and roughly — or, in the passive, put people in each other's company by chance.
examples: I threw together a salad from whatever was left.
He threw a presentation together in twenty minutes.
It looks thrown together, because it was.
Throw it together and we'll fix the details later.
The two of them were thrown together on a project and never separated.

senses.head: Assemble quickly
body: A meal, a deck, an outfit. (сколотить, состряпать на скорую руку)
examples: I threw together a salad from whatever was left.
He threw a presentation together in twenty minutes.
It looks thrown together, because it was.
Throw it together and we'll fix the details later.

senses.head: Bring people into contact by chance
body: Usually passive. (свести (о людях))
examples: The two of them were thrown together on a project and never separated.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: состряпать на скорую руку; свести (людей вместе)
entries.separable: yes — throw together a salad or throw a salad together, and a pronoun must split: throw it together, never ✗ throw together it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 2 (chance acquaintance) is close to a change of state but still reports an event.
entries.passive: yes — a presentation was thrown together in twenty minutes, and sense 2 is effectively passive-only: the two of them were thrown together on a project. The participle is adjectival too: it looks thrown together.

entries.meaning: Vomit; also, put something up in a hurry, or turn something up that nobody expected.
examples: He threw up twice on the flight.
She felt like she was going to throw up.
Developers threw up forty houses in a year.
They threw a fence up over the weekend.
The builders threw them up in under a year.
The search threw up three names we hadn't seen.
The audit threw some awkward questions up.
He threw up his hands and walked out.

senses.head: Vomit
body: Informal but not rude; the clinical word is vomit, and be sick in this meaning is British. (вырвать, стошнить)
examples: He threw up twice on the flight.
She felt like she was going to throw up.

senses.head: Put up hastily
body: Build fast and badly. (наспех возвести)
examples: Developers threw up forty houses in a year.
They threw a fence up over the weekend.
The builders threw them up in under a year.

senses.head: Produce or reveal
body: Of a search, an inquiry, an audit. (выдать, выявить)
examples: The search threw up three names we hadn't seen.
The audit threw some awkward questions up.

senses.head: Throw up one's hands
body: Give up in visible frustration. (развести руками, махнуть рукой)
examples: He threw up his hands and walked out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.русский: вырвать, стошнить; наспех возвести; выявить, породить
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — throw up a fence or throw a fence up, and a pronoun must split: throw it up, never ✗ throw up it. In the "vomit" sense there is usually no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive when it means vomit, transitive in the other senses
entries.verb type: action — dynamic everywhere: vomiting, building fast, turning up a result.
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the transitive senses (forty houses were thrown up in a year, three names we hadn't seen were thrown up by the search); no in the vomit sense, which has no object, and none for the idiom: ✗ his hands were thrown up.

entries.meaning: Force a duty, a role, or an unwanted honor on someone who never asked for it. Most often passive.
examples: The role was thrust upon her when the director resigned.
Nobody asked for the job; it was thrust upon him.
They thrust the whole decision upon a committee that had met twice.
Some have greatness thrust upon them.
He resented having the family business thrust upon him at twenty-two.
Nobody wanted the chairmanship, so the committee thrust it upon the youngest partner.
entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.type: prepositional verb (verb + preposition), with the object fixed in the middle
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — the thing forced sits between thrust and upon, and the person follows: thrust the job upon me, thrust it upon me. A pronoun can go nowhere else: ✗ thrust upon me it. The plainer on works too: thrust the job on me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and formal: forcing a role or a duty on someone who did not ask for it.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the normal form — the role was thrust upon her when the director resigned, some have greatness thrust upon them.

entries.meaning: Step on something — though an American normally says step on — and, figuratively, intrude where you are not wanted.
examples: Careful — you're treading on the flowers.
Somebody trod on my foot in the crowd.
He didn't want to tread on anyone's toes by asking.
The new manager treads on a lot of toes.
She's touchy about it, so don't tread on that ground.

senses.head: Step on
body: Literal. In everyday American speech step on is the ordinary choice; tread on sounds British or bookish. The past is trod here, not treaded. (наступить на)
examples: Careful — you're treading on the flowers.
Somebody trod on my foot in the crowd.

senses.head: Tread on someone's toes
body: Encroach on another person's job, territory, or feelings. This is where the phrase survives in American English. (задеть, влезть в чужие дела)
examples: He didn't want to tread on anyone's toes by asking.
The new manager treads on a lot of toes.
She's touchy about it, so don't tread on that ground.

entries.pronunciation note: in a prepositional verb the verb keeps the stress; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: наступить на; задеть, обидеть, влезть в чужое
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: tread on the flowers, tread on them. ✗ tread the flowers on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; the literal one is British-leaning, since an American says step on.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive works best in the idiom (nobody likes having their toes trodden on); the literal my foot was trodden on is grammatical but bookish in American English, where somebody stepped on my foot is the live sentence.

entries.meaning: Stop sleeping, rouse somebody else, or finally become alert to what is going on.
examples: I woke up at four and couldn't get back to sleep.
Wake me up if the delivery comes.
Don't wake the baby up.
She woke up her whole floor slamming the door.
Wake up — nobody is coming to fix this for you.
The company finally woke up and cut prices.

senses.head: Stop sleeping
body: Intransitive. (просыпаться)
examples: I woke up at four and couldn't get back to sleep.

senses.head: Rouse someone
body: Transitive, and this is where the object placement matters. (будить)
examples: Wake me up if the delivery comes.
Don't wake the baby up.
She woke up her whole floor slamming the door.

senses.head: Become alert or aware
body: Often an imperative aimed at someone being complacent. (очнуться, встряхнуться)
examples: Wake up — nobody is coming to fix this for you.
The company finally woke up and cut prices.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — wake up the kids or wake the kids up, and a pronoun must split: wake me up, never ✗ wake up me. Used of yourself it takes no object at all: I woke up at four.
entries.transitive: either — intransitive when you stop sleeping, transitive when you rouse someone else
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; senses 1 and 3 are inchoative (entering wakefulness or awareness), sense 2 is causative — you make someone else do it.
entries.passive: restricted — only the causative sense passivizes: I was woken up by the delivery truck, the whole floor was woken up. The intransitive senses have no object and so no passive: ✗ it was woken up at four.

entries.meaning: Finally become aware of something that has been true all along. The literal sense — what greets you on waking — is alive too.
examples: The industry is only now waking up to the problem.
He woke up to the fact that nobody was going to help him.
Voters woke up to what the bill actually did.
We woke up to six inches of snow.
She never woke up to how much he was taking.
entries.pronunciation note: the first particle carries the stress
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase: woke up to the risk, woke up to it. ✗ woke the risk up to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inchoative: the moment awareness arrives, not the state of knowing. The progressive is fine: the industry is only now waking up to the problem.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is unavailable here: ✗ the problem is being woken up to by the industry, ✗ six inches of snow was woken up to.

entries.meaning: Remove, or be removed, little by little through rubbing, weather, or time.
examples: The lettering has worn away almost completely.
Water wore the stone away over centuries.
Salt wears the paint away fast around here.
Wear it away slowly with fine sandpaper.
The path wore away to bare dirt by August.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — wear away the stone or wear the stone away, and a pronoun must split: wear it away, never ✗ wear away it. Used of the thing itself it takes no object: the lettering wore away.
entries.transitive: either — transitive for what does the wearing, intransitive for what is worn
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and gradual; the intransitive use is the inchoative twin of the transitive (the lettering wore away ≈ something wore it away).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the stone had been worn away by centuries of water, the lettering has been worn away. The intransitive use has no object and so no passive: ✗ the path was worn away to bare dirt by itself.
entries.see also: wear down, wear off, wear out

entries.meaning: Reduce something by friction — or reduce a person's resistance by simply not stopping.
examples: The heels are worn down on one side.
Years of typing wore the letters down to blanks.
The kids wore me down until I said yes.
Their lawyers just wear you down.
He wore down the opposition with sheer persistence.

senses.head: Reduce by friction
body: Heels, treads, letters on a keyboard. (стачивать, стирать)
examples: The heels are worn down on one side.
Years of typing wore the letters down to blanks.

senses.head: Exhaust someone's resistance
body: Win by persistence rather than argument. (измотать, сломить)
examples: The kids wore me down until I said yes.
Their lawyers just wear you down.
He wore down the opposition with sheer persistence.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — wear down the opposition or wear the opposition down, and a pronoun must split: wear me down, never ✗ wear down me.
entries.transitive: either — transitive when something wears a person or a surface down, intransitive when the thing itself wears down
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, and gradual by definition; the participle also works as an adjective after be: the heels are worn down on one side.
entries.passive: yes — the letters were worn down to blanks by years of typing, I was worn down until I said yes. No passive of the intransitive the treads wore down.
entries.see also: wear out, wear away, win over

entries.meaning: Make new shoes or gear comfortable by using them. Americans say break in: break in a new pair of boots.
examples: Give the boots a week to wear in.
She wore the new shoes in around the house first.
Wear them in before the hike.
A stiff glove needs wearing in.
In the US you'd break them in instead.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — wear in the boots or wear the boots in, and a pronoun must split: wear them in, never ✗ wear in them.
entries.transitive: either — transitive with an object, intransitive of the thing itself: the boots will wear in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and British; the American equivalent is break in. The intransitive use (the boots will wear in) is the same event told from the object's side.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the shoes were worn in around the house first, a stiff glove needs to be worn in. None for the intransitive.

entries.meaning: Gradually stop having an effect.
examples: The anesthetic started to wear off an hour later.
The novelty wore off fast.
Give it a minute — the sting will wear off.
By noon the caffeine had worn off.
His enthusiasm wore off the second he saw the schedule.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place: the novelty wore off, never ✗ wore the novelty off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, gradual, and intransitive: an effect fading, not a state. The progressive is natural: the anesthetic is wearing off.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote: ✗ the novelty was worn off, ✗ the caffeine had been worn off by noon.
entries.see also: wear away, wear out, wake up

entries.meaning: Of time, to pass slowly; of noise, work, or a person, to grind someone down.
examples: As the evening wore on, people started leaving.
The meeting wore on for another hour.
His voice really wears on me.
The commute started to wear on her.
Twelve-hour shifts wear on you after a while.

senses.head: Pass slowly
